source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning?
finding: Design: a two-trap trap-tube. The crow must pull meat out of the tube on the side that avoids a hole (trap). Success is first shown on the training tube, then on step-by-step transfers that remove arbitrary cues, then on a visually different trap-table. Each transfer strips one low-level explanation.
numbers: 6 wild crows. 3 of 6 (Obo, Tiga, Slevin) solved the initial tube in under 150 trials, mean 103.3 +/- 20.3 trials. Criterion on training tube: 17 of 20 correct over two blocks (binomial alpha 0.01). Transfer criterion: 15 of 20 (alpha 0.05), or 9 of 10 in the first block.
quote: arbitrary features that had previously been associated with successful performances were removed
limits: Only 3 crows passed; the 3 failures are used later as a control. One lab, one species.
agent_relevance: The control logic is a ladder: remove one cue per transfer, then test a task that shares only the causal structure. Our held-out checks can use the same ladder.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? (transfers 1 and 2: single arbitrary cues)
finding: Transfer 1 removed the two yellow discs (blue rim kept). Transfer 2 removed the blue rim and recoloured the discs black. All three crows still avoided the trap in both. So no single arbitrary cue explained success.
numbers: 3 of 3 crows passed transfer 1 and transfer 2 (15 of 20 or better).
limits: Passing both does not exclude a bundle of independent cue rules (e.g. pull away from blue rim OR toward high disc). That is why the authors added transfer 3 and the trap-table.
agent_relevance: A single held-out variant is weak. A suite of variants, each removing a different cue, is needed to exclude cue bundles.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? (transfer 3: two holes)
finding: Transfer 3 had one functional trap (hole with a base) and one non-functional trap (a bare hole). All three crows failed. They were reluctant to pull food into either hole. This shows they used the hole, not the trap base, as the causal feature. It is a negative result that limits the claim.
numbers: 3 of 3 crows failed. Latency and side-switching were highest in transfer 3 for all 3 crows (binomial p = 0.0156 against a 0.25 chance per crow). Tiga and Slevin avoided the trap on trial 1 of transfer 3, then performed at chance in the next 19 trials.
limits: A failed transfer is informative: it narrows what the animal knows (a proximate hole rule, not gravity). The authors call the reasoning intermediate between weak and strong causal knowledge.
agent_relevance: Report held-out failures as precisely as passes. A failure on a structured variant tells us which rule the agent actually holds.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? (trap-table: visually distinct, causally equivalent)
finding: The trap-table differs from the tube in shape, colour and material. All three successful crows solved it and chose correctly on their very first trial. This is the central control against associative learning and visual or tactile generalisation. The 3 crows that failed the tube also failed the table, which rules out a prior disposition to avoid holes.
numbers: 3 of 3 successful crows solved the table, correct on trial 1. 3 of 3 tube-failures failed the table. Across all 4 transfers, 10 of 12 first trials were correct. In 10 of 12 first trials neither the surface nor the trap was probed, which argues against tactile generalisation.
quote: it was unlikely that any associative rules ... could be generalized from the trap-tube to trap-table
limits: Authors rely on Shepard's generalisation law (more perceptual distance, less generalisation). That is an argument, not a measure of perceptual distance. Only 3 birds.
agent_relevance: The best control is a task that shares only the relational structure with the training task. For our agent, held-out items should change surface form while keeping the rule.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? (chance and first-trial analysis)
finding: The authors tested a chance account: the crow guesses on trial 1 of each transfer, then repeats whatever worked. They show first-trial success did not predict later success, and that tracking random side switches would not fit the 100+ trials needed to learn the first tube.
numbers: First trials: 10 of 12 correct. Tiga erred on trial 1 of transfer 2, then avoided the trap in the next 19 trials. Tiga and Slevin were right on trial 1 of transfer 3 but at chance for the next 19.
limits: Twelve first trials is a small sample. First-trial analysis is a weak test alone.
agent_relevance: Check first-attempt accuracy and later accuracy separately. A pass that does not persist, or persists without a first pass, signals a different mechanism.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? (framework: triangulation, Heyes 1993)
finding: Method named 'triangulation' (Heyes 1993): train on one task, then transfer with arbitrary stimuli changed and causal structure held fixed. Success across transfers eliminates cue-based rules. The paper explains why an associative cue can only reach a new problem through perceptual similarity (Spence 1937; Shepard 1987), while causal knowledge can transfer by analogy (Goswami and Brown 1989; Gentner 1983).
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Triangulation is a design principle, not a proof. The authors still end at 'unlikely', not 'ruled out'.
agent_relevance: This is the core method for our G3: vary the arbitrary, hold the structure fixed, and ask which hypotheses survive each variant.

source: Martin-Ordas, Call, Colmenares (2008) Tubes, tables and traps: great apes solve two functionally equivalent trap tasks but show no evidence of transfer across tasks
finding: 20 great apes (6 orangutans, 6 chimpanzees, 5 bonobos, 3 gorillas) did a trap-platform task and a trap-tube task. They solved each, but success on one did not predict success on the other. This is the contrast with the crow transfer.
numbers: 12 of 20 solved the platform; 8 of 20 solved the tube. 5 solved both, 7 platform only, 3 tube only, 5 neither. Correlation between tasks r = 0.13, p = 0.57, n = 20. Platform better than tube: F(1,16) = 3.46, p = 0.04 one-tailed. First trial: platform 14/20 (p = 0.074), tube 12/20 (p = 0.37). Prior trap experience had no effect (t(18) = 0.35).
limits: Platform and tube differ in difficulty and action affordances (apes prefer raking). Failure to transfer may mean knowledge bound to actions, not absence of causal knowledge.
agent_relevance: Absence of transfer is ambiguous: no causal knowledge, or knowledge bound to the format. A failed held-out check needs a diagnostic follow-up before any conclusion.

source: Visalberghi and Limongelli (1994); Povinelli (2000); Silva et al. (2005) trap-tube founding work, as described in Martin-Ordas et al. 2008
finding: Founding trap-tube work. Capuchins: after 120 trials 1 of 4 solved by pushing food away from the trap, but kept doing so when the trap was inverted (non-functional). This was read as a distance rule without causal understanding. Povinelli 2000 repeated this with chimpanzees.
numbers: Capuchins: 1 of 4 solved after 120 trials. Povinelli: only 1 chimpanzee avoided the trap and also acted as if the inverted trap were functional. (Secondhand from the Martin-Ordas 2008 introduction; originals not opened.)
limits: Silva et al. 2005 showed adult humans also avoid the inverted trap when avoidance is free, so the inverted-trap control is conceptually flawed. Push-only tools may have masked knowledge (Mulcahy and Call 2006).
agent_relevance: A control can itself be invalid. Check that the 'wrong' response in the control has a real cost, otherwise passing it proves nothing.

source: Seed, Tebbich, Emery, Clayton (2006) Investigating physical cognition in rooks; Tebbich et al. (2007), as described in Martin-Ordas 2008
finding: Rooks with a two-trap tube, which removes the need for an inverted-trap control. 7 of 8 rooks solved and transferred to a similar tube, but 6 of 7 failed two transfer tasks with no shared visual constant. One passed. In the 2007 study with a one-trap tube, 3 of 7 solved and none passed the transfers.
numbers: 7 of 8 solved; 6 of 7 failed far transfers; 1 passed. Tebbich 2007: 3 of 7 solved, 0 transfer. (Secondhand from Martin-Ordas 2008; the Cell site blocked the original.)
limits: Single successful bird; the transfers required opposite responses to familiar cues, unlike the crow design of removing features step by step.
agent_relevance: One individual passing is suggestive only. Replication across individuals is part of the control, not an extra.

source: Taylor, Medina, Holzhaider, Hearne, Hunt, Gray (2010) An investigation into the cognition behind spontaneous string pulling in New Caledonian crows
finding: Alternative explanation tested: that 'insight' string pulling is operant conditioning through a perceptual-motor feedback loop. The authors blocked visual feedback and gave a mirror to restore it. Experienced crows did worse without feedback; naive crows failed or used trial and error; a mirror restored performance.
numbers: 4 experienced crows: 3 of 4 obtained meat on trial 1; pull-step ratio fell from 96.5% to 55.7% when vision was restricted; errors rose about 10-fold (Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum possible with n = 4). Naive: 1 of 4 solved (Angel, trial 5), 3 never. With mirror: 2 of 4 solved (Slevin trial 3, Ronia trial 5).
limits: Tiny samples (n = 4 per group). This manipulates the rival mechanism's input, a different kind of control from transfer.
agent_relevance: To test whether behaviour depends on a low-level mechanism, remove that mechanism's input and see if performance collapses. Analogue: remove the cheap cue from the agent's input.

source: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt, Gray (2010) Complex cognition and behavioural innovation in New Caledonian crows
finding: Three-stage metatool problem (string, short stick, long stick in toolbox, food). Crows linked learned behaviours into a novel sequence on trial 1. The authors argue against resurgence, chaining, conditional reinforcement and the Epstein competition-of-repertoires account, using an innovation group with no prior experience of the components.
numbers: Component group: 3 of 3 solved on trial 1 without error. Innovation group (n = 4): 2 solved on trial 1 (Sam error-free after 110 s inspection; Caspar after pulling and dropping the string), Maya on trial 3, Djinn on trial 4.
limits: Only 1 of 4 innovation crows was clearly spontaneous. Arguments against each rival rest on predictions about extinction and resurgence, not direct tests. Small n.
agent_relevance: Each rival mechanism is given a concrete prediction (resurgence predicts re-probing the hole; crows probed the toolbox first). Write the rival's prediction down before running the check.

source: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt, Gray (2010) (competing-mechanism logic)
finding: The paper lists simple mechanisms that could produce a novel sequence and tests each against the data: conditional reinforcement (the short stick became punishing, so it predicts the behaviour dies out), chaining (needs training on each component), resurgence (predicts re-probing the hole), and a propensity to pull strings and probe dark places.
numbers: Training with the short stick (innovation group): crows first stopped probing (mean 5.25 trials, range 2-7), then discarded the short tool (mean 2 trials), then ignored it (mean 2.75 trials). Despite this, all 4 later used it as a metatool. In the 2007 study, 6 of 7 crows probed the toolbox first.
limits: The conditioning story is argued from history; no direct manipulation of reinforcement.
agent_relevance: Enumerate the cheap explanations, then derive one differential prediction per explanation. This is the template for an alternative-explanation checklist.

source: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt, Emery, Clayton, Gray (2011) New Caledonian crows learn the functional properties of novel tool types (arbitrary-link control)
finding: A clean associative control: re-run the same discrimination with an arbitrary instead of a causal link between object and reward. Associative learning should not care. The crows learned fast when the link was causal (stone dropping) and not when arbitrary (search task).
numbers: Large vs. small stone: 88% large in the first 20 drops, versus 46% in the matched search task (chi2(1) = 6.13, p = 0.013). Water vs. sand: 58% vs. 56% at group level (chi2 = 0.0003, p = 0.99), but Laura 90% vs. 55% (chi2(1) = 4.51, p = 0.034). 4 crows in dropping, 3 in search.
quote: It should be irrelevant to a simple associative account whether these correlations are arbitrary or causal.
limits: The water vs. sand group difference was not significant; the claim rests on the stone result and one bird. Search tasks differ from dropping tasks in procedure as well.
agent_relevance: Match the control task to the test task on everything except the causal link. That isolates whether the model uses the relevant structure or just covariation.

source: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt, Emery, Clayton, Gray (2011) New Caledonian crows learn the functional properties of novel tool types (first-trial preferences)
finding: Evidence that crows used functional properties before seeing outcomes: some picked up and discarded small stones, light blocks and non-functional objects on the very first trial.
numbers: Small stone discarded 62% of pickups in the first 5 trials. Water over sand 61% (p = 0.048); water over air 60% (p = 0.042); heavy rubber over light polystyrene 65% (p = 0.009). On trial 1, rubber dropped 100% of pickups vs. polystyrene 46%; over the first 5 trials 88% vs 40% (chi2 = 25.76).
limits: Preferences for object features (solid, stone-like) can be prior biases (see Logan 2014). Counts are small. Learning from earlier accidental drops is not excluded.
agent_relevance: Separate first-attempt behaviour (before feedback) from learned behaviour. First-attempt accuracy on a new instance is a better knowledge test than accuracy after feedback.

source: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt, Emery, Clayton, Gray (2011) New Caledonian crows learn the functional properties of novel tool types (no transfer to sticks)
finding: Preferences for heavy or voluminous objects did not carry over to stick tools (Experiments 9 and 10). Knowledge from stone dropping did not generalise across mechanically different tasks.
numbers: Exp 9: light and heavy tools each used 46% of 26 probes (chi2 = 0.77, p = 0.78); string used 7%. Exp 10: 59% of 22 probes used the small-diameter tool (binomial p = 0.52).
limits: A null transfer: shows specificity, which argues against a simple object-weight rule, but also limits generality.
agent_relevance: Narrow rules that do not generalise are a sign of task-level knowledge. Expect the same in an agent.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton, Gray (2014) Using the Aesop's fable paradigm to investigate causal understanding of water displacement by New Caledonian crows
finding: Six experiments on water displacement. Crows succeeded on four (water vs. sand, sinking vs. floating, solid vs. hollow, high vs. low water) and failed on two (narrow vs. wide tube; U-tube with a hidden connection). Success is compared with 5 to 7 year old children.
numbers: Exp1 water vs sand: 76.3% water (binomial p = 0.001). Exp2 sinking 88.0% (p < 0.001), floating discarded 65% of pickups. Exp3 solid 89.0% (p < 0.001). Exp5 wide/high 86.8% (p < 0.001). Exp4 narrow tube 39.3% of drops, first drop 56% narrow (p = 0.27). Exp6 U-tube 48.9% (p = 0.79). 6 birds in exp 1-2, 5 in exp 3-4, 4 in exp 5-6.
limits: Fixed task order, so earlier tasks may have helped later ones (authors admit). Small sample; not all birds finished all tasks.
agent_relevance: Report passes and fails together; the pattern of failures exposes the real rule. A hidden-mechanism test (U-tube) is the hardest class.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances (colour-cue confound in the U-tube)
finding: A replication and extension that found a new alternative explanation. One crow (Kitty) passed a coloured U-tube, but all crows failed an uncovered U-tube with the connector visible. The authors conclude Kitty's pass was a colour-cue association, not inference of a hidden mechanism.
numbers: Coloured U-tube: 1 of 5 birds passed (connected tube chosen 47% overall). Uncovered U-tube: 0 of 5 passed (44%). Kitty chose correctly on trial 1 of the uncovered tube but not consistently.
limits: Small n; some birds did not finish. The colour-association reading is an inference, not measured.
agent_relevance: When a pass appears, build the variant that removes the suspected cue and see whether the pass survives. This is a held-out mutation of the input.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances (object-bias control: no water)
finding: A control earlier studies lacked: a platform task with no water. Crows still chose solid over hollow objects 95% of the time. So the apparent solidity understanding in water tasks may be a handling or object preference.
numbers: Platform solid vs hollow: 5 of 5 birds p < 0.001, 95% of objects dropped were solid (3 had no prior water experience). Water tasks: 6 of 6 passed solid vs hollow (95%). First choices on trial 1 for exps 1-3 combined: 15 of 17 correct (p = 0.002). Volume first-trial: 5 of 10 (p = 1.00).
limits: Authors call for further work. Only solid vs hollow showed no learning effect, which fits a pre-existing bias.
agent_relevance: Test whether the 'correct' option is favoured for reasons unrelated to the task. Run the cue-only version without the task.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances (volume and learning curves)
finding: With fewer objects available (four, not twelve), 4 of 6 crows chose the narrow tube, and 3 of those switched to the wide tube when its water was higher. The switch shows it was not a fixed narrow-tube preference. It may still reflect feedback tracking, and the authors say so.
numbers: Exp4 narrow chosen 64% of the time (4 of 6 passed, 2 failed). Exp5: 3 of the 4 switched to wide (79%).
limits: Visual feedback and mental modelling are not separated; the authors ask for a no-feedback tube.
agent_relevance: A reversal condition (the preference must flip when the rule flips) is a strong control against fixed preferences.

source: Taylor, Miller, Gray (2012) New Caledonian crows reason about hidden causal agents
finding: Eight crows watched a stick move from a hide, either after a human entered the hide and left (HCA) or with no human entering (UCA). Two rival hypotheses: habituation (caution falls with exposure) versus causal reasoning (caution stays high if no agent explains the movement). Hide inspection was higher in UCA.
numbers: n = 8. Inspection UCA > HCA: Wilcoxon Z = 3.171, p = 0.002; first trial Z = 2.521, p = 0.008; second trial p = 0.008; third trial p = 0.547. Last habituation vs first HCA: p = 0.945. 4 of 8 crows abandoned probing in UCA (mean 2.75 +/- 1.03); 0 in HCA.
limits: Fixed order HCA before UCA (no counterbalance); the human entering and leaving could be a conditioned cue (Boogert et al. 2013; Dymond et al. 2013). See the failed replication.
agent_relevance: Condition order and cue confounds can mimic a cognitive effect. Counterbalance and add a non-threatening cue control.

source: O'Neill et al. (2021) New Caledonian crows and hidden causal agents revisited
finding: Failed replication of Taylor et al. 2012 with 14 new crows and three added control groups (counterbalanced order, associative-cue controls). The direct replication did not reproduce the effect, so the other groups could not be interpreted. Conclusion: neither supports nor refutes hidden-agent reasoning.
numbers: Direct replication n = 4: HCA M = 8.69 vs UCA M = 10.95 hide inspections per min; paired t(3) = -2.16, p = .12. First trials 11.93 vs 8.77, p = .21. Reverse order n = 4: 7.52 vs 9.26, p = .42. Pooled: Wilcoxon V = 7, p = .15. Pooled first trial vs pre-test: V = 34, p = .023 (a novelty effect, not a condition effect).
limits: Low power (4 birds per group); different wild-caught birds and years. The authors cannot separate low power from a real difference.
agent_relevance: A pass that does not replicate on an independent sample says the check is fragile. Run key checks on fresh samples before relying on them.

source: Boogert et al. (2013) and Dymond et al. (2013) commentaries on Taylor et al. 2012, as described in O'Neill et al. 2021
finding: Two commentaries listed missing controls: no counterbalanced order, so sensitisation to an aversive stimulus could explain rising vigilance (Dymond); and the human entering and leaving may only be a conditioned stimulus marking when the stick attack starts and stops (Boogert). Also the human operating the stick may not have been blind.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative criticisms. (Secondhand from the O'Neill introduction; commentaries not opened.)
limits: Criticisms are logical, not empirical; the replication did not clearly resolve them.
agent_relevance: Turn each criticism into a named control: order counterbalance, cue-only control, blind operator. A checklist of these is reusable.

source: Gruber et al. (2019) New Caledonian crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems
finding: A redesign that removes the usual alternative explanations (chaining, perceptual-motor feedback loops): each stage is out of sight of the others, and distractors (a non-functional tool or apparatus) are added. Some crows solved three stages. In 2018 an online-planning route was excluded by counting inspect-while-holding-a-tool as an error.
numbers: Exp1: 14 crows; of 11 given the stick problem first, 4 reached 16/20 with few errors and 4 more by trial 43. Stone problem: 4 of 11 reached criterion by trial 46. Exp2: 3 of 8 within 60 trials (25, 26, 39), Mercury at 69. Exp3: 3 of 3 passed the stick condition (18, 17, 16 of 20); 1 passed stone within 60. Preplanning check: Aretha 12/14 (p = 0.013), Freddie 14/18 (p = 0.031); 2018 Saturn 20/20, Triton 16/20.
quote: crows were able to mentally represent the sub-goals and goals of metatool problems
limits: Many crows failed and needed considerable experience; criterion 16/20 is the authors' choice; 'conclusive' is stronger than the samples support; Exp 3 had 3 birds.
agent_relevance: Redesign the check so the cheap strategy is impossible, add distractors that a cue-follower would choose, then count how many individuals still pass.

source: Heyes (2012) Simple minds: a qualified defence of associative learning
finding: Argues that both 'association-blindness' (never considering associative learning) and 'simple-mindedness' (assuming associative explanations win by default, via Morgan's canon) are mistakes. No shortcut: spell out each explanation in enough detail to make differential predictions, then test them.
numbers: No new numbers. Case study is chimpanzee cooperation.
quote: there are no short-cuts to finding out about animal minds
limits: Argument from history and philosophy of science, not data. It criticises the justifications of Morgan's canon (simplicity, evolution).
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'it is memorisation or pattern matching' as the default winner, and do not treat 'it reasoned' as a default either. State both with testable predictions.

source: Wu et al. (2023/2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks
finding: Direct LLM analogue of the transfer control. Take tasks models do well (default) and change the world's rules while keeping the reasoning procedure the same (counterfactual). 11 tasks; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2. Counterfactual performance is consistently lower than default but usually above chance.
numbers: 11 tasks. Arithmetic: 1000 two-digit additions in bases 8, 9, 10, 11, 16 (non-10 bases checked to differ from base-10 results). Code tasks use 1-based indexing (113 discriminating test cases for generation). Default and counterfactual performance are correlated; 0-shot CoT does not close the gap. Per-cell accuracies are in appendix tables, not extracted here.
limits: Authors list underestimation risks (the counterfactual may be harder for reasons other than reasoning) and possible overlap with training data.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual comprehension check (CCC): first check the model understands the new rule (e.g. the next integer in base 9), then test the task. This controls for 'failed because it did not grasp the rules' and applies directly to our held-out checks.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024/2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in large language models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Template-based variants of GSM8K (new names and numbers) show performance varies across instantiations and falls on new numbers. Adding a distractor clause that looks relevant but changes nothing (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops. The original 100 questions often sit at the upper edge of the distribution, which suggests contamination.
numbers: 100 templates x 50 samples = 5000 questions per benchmark; 8-shot CoT. Means (GSM-Symbolic to NoOp): GPT-4o 94.9 to 63.1; o1-mini 94.5 to 66.0; o1-preview 92.7 to 77.4; GPT-4o-mini 91.7 to 54.1; Llama3-8b-instruct 74.6 to 18.6. Gemma2-9b-it: GSM8K 87.0, GSM-Symbolic 79.1 (sd 3.0). Original question score lies beyond 1 sd in 21 of 25 models. Up to 65% drop on NoOp. GPT-4o with added clauses: 94.9 (Symbolic), 93.9 (P1), 88.0 (P2).
limits: The 'no genuine reasoning' conclusion is the authors' hypothesis. 8 shots of the same NoOp question did not fix it.
agent_relevance: A distractor-clause mutation is an easy held-out check for G3: add irrelevant but plausible content and see if the answer changes. Also compare original items with fresh instances.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Takes the Kosinski vignettes where GPT-3.5 appeared to pass false-belief tests and makes small changes that keep the ToM principle (transparent container, informed protagonist). Outputs flip to the wrong answer. Argues the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation should be skeptical and that failures should outweigh average success.
numbers: Original: P(chocolate) = 99% (belief prompt 1), 82% (prompt 2). Transparent bag: P(chocolate) = 95% for 'She believes that the bag is full of' (wrong); for prompt 2 popcorn 58% vs chocolate 36% (an earlier version reported a flip, later traced to a double-space prompt artefact). Transparent chest: John thinks the cat is in the chest 94%, will look in the chest 90%.
quote: the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation in intuitive psychology should be skeptical
limits: One model (GPT-3.5); small hand-made variant set; a whitespace change altered a result, showing prompt sensitivity. Later models may do better.
agent_relevance: Use small, principle-preserving variants as held-out checks, and pin prompt formatting because checks can be brittle.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or neural theory-of-mind? Stress testing social reasoning in large language models
finding: Six ToM tasks with adversarial variants. LLMs show some ToM-like ability but it is not robust; they fail when adversarial examples change the surface. The authors infer reliance on shallow heuristics.
numbers: GPT-4 reaches 97% on the original false-belief subset but fails on adversarial transparent-access and relationship-change items. 6 tasks, two probing formats (generative QA vs. answer-choice probability).
limits: Per-variant accuracies not extracted. 'Shallow heuristics' is an interpretation. Models from mid-2023.
agent_relevance: A high score on the standard set and a low score on adversarial variants means the standard check was effectively fitted to. Keep both sets.

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2023/2024) Embers of autoregression: understanding large language models through the problem they are trained to solve
finding: Alternative explanation applied to LLMs: accuracy depends on the probability of the task, the target output and the input, even in deterministic tasks. 11 tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Failures appear when the correct answer is low-probability text.
numbers: GPT-4 cipher decoding: 51% accuracy when the output is a high-probability word sequence, 13% when low-probability. Another setting: 21% vs 11% by input probability. Shift-13 cipher is over 100 times more common in text than shift-12, and GPT-4 does better on it.
limits: Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613); 11 tasks. Later models may differ.
agent_relevance: A pass may come from familiarity of the answer. For G3, include checks whose correct answer is unlikely text (rare symbols, odd shifts).

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Applies the counterfactual design to letter-string analogies reported as solved by GPT-3 (Webb et al. 2023). Permuted or symbol alphabets leave humans high but cut GPT accuracy sharply. A counterfactual comprehension check shows the models mostly understand the new orderings.
numbers: Webb et al. had 57 UCLA undergraduates; the new human sample scored higher with a similar pattern. 70 samples per point (new data) vs 100 (Webb). CCC accuracy generally high, exception GPT-3.5 on 'predecessor' with 2 or 5 letters permuted.
limits: Per-model accuracy numbers not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Analogy checks should be re-run with the surface changed. Keep a human reference when available.
